references.text: Matthew's version of the Golden Rule: 'Do to others what you would have them do to you. For this is the law and the prophets.' This is the parallel passage in the Sermon on the Mount.
'Love your neighbor as yourself.' This command from the Mosaic Law is the foundation for the Golden Rule that Jesus formulates in Luke 6:31.
Jesus identifies love for one's neighbor as the second greatest commandment, which aligns with the Golden Rule of treating others as you wish to be treated.
Paul summarizes the law in the command to love: whoever loves their neighbor has fulfilled the law. This reflects the principle of the Golden Rule to do good to others.
Paul states that the entire law is fulfilled in this one command: 'Love your neighbor as yourself.' This encapsulates the same principle as the Golden Rule.
Paul urges believers not to act out of selfish ambition, but in humility to value others above themselves and look to their interests—an practical expression of the Golden Rule.
Jesus' command to love enemies and do good to those who hate you extends the Golden Rule to include even those who do not return kindness.
The immediate context before the Golden Rule: Jesus speaks about loving enemies, doing good to those who hate you, and giving to those who ask—all forming the background for verse 31.
'Do not say, 'As he has done to me, so I will do to him.' Proverbs warns against retaliation and points toward the principle of treating others fairly.
'The foreigner living among you shall be like one of your own, and you shall love them as yourself.' This Old Testament command extends neighborly love to all, just as the Golden Rule does.
